profile.name: Para Para
profile.tagline: Synchronized Japanese dance with choreographed arm movements to Eurobeat music
profile.insight: In 1999, Takuya Kimura's TV dance to 'Night of Fire' sparked Para Para's third boom, spreading its popularity beyond Japan.
profile.profile: Para Para is a Japanese synchronized group dance featuring choreographed upper body movements to Eurobeat music, with minimal footwork. Each song has a specific routine, learned and performed in clubs and communities worldwide. The dance evolved through four popularity booms since the 1980s, with official and 'maniac' routines created by club-affiliated choreographers. Variants include TechPara and TraPara, danced to techno and trance music respectively.
profile.profile_long:
Para Para is a synchronized dance that originated in Japan in the early 1980s, characterized by choreographed arm and hand movements performed in unison to Eurobeat music, a fast-paced electronic genre with roots in Italo disco and Euro disco. Unlike typical club or rave dances, Para Para features specific routines for each song, similar to line dancing, with dancers stepping side to side and moving hips but with limited lower body movement. The dance's name is believed to derive from the onomatopoeic sound of hand movements matching the music's beat.

The dance likely developed from two main origins: men choreographing dances in VIP club rooms to impress women, and the Takenoko-zoku youth subculture that danced choreographed routines in Harajuku's Yoyogi Park pedestrian plaza in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Para Para's history is marked by four distinct booms of popularity. The first boom (1987–1992) occurred in high-class discos during Japan's bubble economy, with routines difficult to trace due to scarce recordings. The 'wangan' style emerged around Tokyo Bay clubs circa 1993.

The second boom (1993–1995) saw many routines originate from popular clubs like Xenon and Twinstar. Avex Trax released one of the first official Para Para videos in 1994, containing 40 routines still used today. The third boom (1999–2001) was catalyzed by Takuya Kimura's televised performance on SMAP×SMAP, popularizing Para Para nationally and internationally. Commercial videos and idol groups like ParaPara Allstars emerged, and 'maniac' unofficial routines appeared.

The fourth boom (2005–2010) featured aggressive marketing by Avex with DVDs and anime-themed Eurobeat remixes, peaking around 2007–2009. After 2010, commercial releases declined, leading to a glacial period with fewer new dancers and smaller club events. The internet, especially YouTube, became vital for sharing lessons and routines.

Para Para is danced mainly to Eurobeat but also has variants like TechPara (hyper techno) and TraPara (trance). Official routines are choreographed by groups affiliated with clubs such as Starfire, SEF, and Twinstar, while 'maniac' routines are unofficial and less common today. The dance community is global, with active groups in Japan, Chile, Brazil, Spain, the US, Canada, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Finland.

Club events typically start with less danceable music before moving to Eurobeat, with lessons teaching new routines. Club videos, once rare and coveted, have become more accessible online. Notable clubs include Twin Star, Velfarre, and Maharaja in Tokyo. Para Para's cultural significance includes its connection to Japanese youth subcultures, club scenes, and international otaku communities.

sections.origins_and_history: Para Para originated in Japan in the early 1980s, influenced by European Italo disco and Euro disco music and the Japanese Takenoko-zoku youth subculture dancing choreographed routines in Harajuku. It developed in VIP club rooms and pedestrian plazas. The dance experienced four booms: the first in late 1980s high-class discos, the second in early 1990s clubs with official videos released by Avex Trax, the third around 1999 boosted by Takuya Kimura's TV appearance, and the fourth in mid-2000s with anime-themed Eurobeat remixes. After 2010, commercial activity declined, but the dance persists online and in smaller events.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Para Para is danced in synchronized groups performing choreographed upper body movements—primarily arms and hands—specific to each song's routine. Dancers step side to side and move hips slightly, with minimal leg movement except for stepping in place or hopping. The rhythm follows a four-on-the-floor beat typical of Eurobeat music. Beginners learn routines through club lessons involving slow, spoken instruction and repetition with and without music. Variants like TechPara and TraPara differ mainly in tempo and complexity of arm and foot movements.
sections.music_and_instruments: Para Para is danced mainly to Eurobeat music, a fast-paced electronic genre derived from Italo disco and Euro disco, characterized by a four-on-the-floor rhythm and upbeat tempo. Variants include TechPara danced to hyper techno and TraPara danced to trance music. Eurobeat tracks often feature synthesizers, electronic drums, and energetic vocals. The dance's music progression in clubs typically moves from early 1990s to late 1990s and 2000s Eurobeat releases.
sections.costume_and_setting: Para Para is primarily danced in club settings in Japan, including notable venues like Twin Star, Velfarre, and Maharaja. Club events often begin with less danceable music and increase in energy. Dancers wear casual or club attire; no specific costume is mandated. The dance community includes official choreographer groups affiliated with clubs. Internationally, Para Para is performed at conventions and cultural events, especially those related to Japanese pop culture.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Para Para is performed at club events, dance lessons, and cultural conventions worldwide. It serves as a social dance fostering community among fans of Eurobeat and Japanese pop culture. The dance's synchronized routines create a shared experience, with lessons preserving and transmitting choreography. It is also featured in competitions and media, reflecting its status as a cultural phenomenon linked to Japanese youth and otaku culture.
sections.notable_figures: Key choreographer groups include Shishō Gundan, known for Twinstar routines, with members like Gori-shishō (Keita Fukaya) and Arai-shishō (Takashi Arai). T-RREX, formed by Twinstar, Rie, Richie, and Xenon members, choreographs for StarFire. Team SEF choreographs exclusively for SEF club events. The idol group ParaPara Allstars, featuring members like Richie and Satoko, was prominent during the third boom. Takuya Kimura's televised dance in 1999 significantly boosted Para Para's popularity.
sections.regional_variants: Variants of Para Para include TechPara, danced to hyper techno music with faster and more complex arm movements, and TraPara (or ToraPara), danced to trance music with slower, more subdued movements. OriPara refers to original routines created by individuals outside official choreographer groups. Maniac routines are unofficial choreographies created by clubs and dancers, mostly in Japan, and have declined since 2008. Internationally, Para Para communities adapt routines and create refilms shared online.
sections.lineage: Para Para descends from Japanese club and street dance cultures of the 1980s, influenced by European Italo disco and Euro disco music. It shares some movement similarities with traditional Japanese Bon Odori and cheering squad dances (Ōendan) but is distinct in its synchronized choreography to Eurobeat. The dance evolved through club scenes and choreographer groups, with official and maniac routines shaping its development. It has influenced and been featured in rhythm games like Para Para Paradise.

claims.text: Para Para is a synchronized dance that originated in Japan featuring specific movements for each song, like line dancing.
claims.quote: Para Para (パラパラ, ParaPara) or Para-Para is a synchronized dance that originated in Japan. Unlike most types of club and rave dancing, Para Para features specific synchronized movements for each song, much like line dancing.

claims.text: The dance began in the early 1980s with the spread of Italo disco and Eurodisco music in Japan.
claims.quote: Para Para has been around since the early 1980s, when European countries started selling Italo disco and Eurodisco and, in the mid-to late 1970s, new wave and synthpop music in Japan.

claims.text: Para Para dancing consists mostly of upper body movements synchronized to a four-on-the-floor rhythm.
claims.quote: Para Para dancing consists of mostly upper body movements in synchronization with a four-on-the-floor rhythm.

claims.text: The dance is strongly associated with Eurobeat music, which is usually very fast.
claims.quote: Para Para is strongly associated with Eurobeat. Eurobeat artist Dave Rodgers has described Para Para as the only way to dance to Eurobeat, which is usually 'so fast.'

claims.text: The third boom of Para Para (1999–2001) was sparked by Takuya Kimura's televised dance to 'Night of Fire'.
claims.quote: The cause of this boom has largely been credited to the appearance of Takuya Kimura on television program SMAP×SMAP, dancing to Niko's 'Night of Fire'.

claims.text: Official Para Para routines are choreographed by club-affiliated groups such as Starfire, SEF, and Twinstar.
claims.quote: The term 'official' in the parapara world describes routines made by certain clubs/choreography groups in Japan. A non-exhaustive list of official club events are Starfire, SEF, 9LoveJ, and Twinstar.

claims.text: Para Para includes variants like TechPara (hyper techno) and TraPara (trance).
claims.quote: Some variants of Para Para include TechPara (set to hyper techno instead of Eurobeat), and TraPara or ToraPara (set to trance).

claims.text: Para Para is danced internationally, with communities in Chile, Brazil, Spain, the US, Canada, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Finland.
claims.quote: Fans of Para Para often refer to themselves as 'paralists' and include official and unofficial teams of dancers in Japan, Chile, Brazil, Spain, the United States, Canada, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Finland, and several other countries.
